title: Sealed Inside, a Receptor Goes Silent

scenes.tts: A macrophage swallows the equivalent of its whole surface about every half hour, and it does not shrink. Every receptor in that membrane makes the trip too. At the surface, the tail of a receptor points into the cell. So where does the receptor go once it is inside? And what does the trip do to its signal?
scenes.visual: A strip of membrane with receptor bars, tails down. One pit deepens under three of them and pinches off as a vesicle while a clock sweeps beside a bracket over the whole surface. The vesicle sinks as the trip is named, the tails are labelled, then a dashed question box and a dashed 'signal ?' appear.
scenes.narration: A macrophage swallows the equivalent of its whole surface about every half hour, and it does not shrink. Every receptor in that membrane makes the trip too. At the surface, the tail of a receptor points into the cell. So where does the receptor go once it is inside? And what does the trip do to its signal?

scenes.tts: A receptor enters a pit because its tail carries a sequence that an adaptor can read. The adaptor links the tail to a coat of clathrin. The pit deepens until it hangs by a thin neck. A protein called dynamin builds a collar around the neck. When it breaks down G T P, the neck is cut and the vesicle is free.
scenes.caption: A receptor enters a pit because its tail carries a sequence that an adaptor can read. The adaptor links the tail to a coat of clathrin. The pit deepens until it hangs by a thin neck. A protein called dynamin builds a collar around the neck. When it breaks down GTP, the neck is cut and the vesicle is free.
scenes.visual: Zoomed on one patch of membrane: a tick on each receptor tail, an adaptor block on each tick, a clathrin coat joining the adaptors. The patch bows into a deep pit that hangs by a neck; two dynamin pieces close on the neck and cut it, and the vesicle drops away.
scenes.narration: A receptor enters a pit because its tail carries a sequence that an adaptor can read. The adaptor links the tail to a coat of clathrin. The pit deepens until it hangs by a thin neck. A protein called dynamin builds a collar around the neck. When it breaks down GTP, the neck is cut and the vesicle is free.

scenes.tts: The vesicle reaches the early endosome, the first stop for almost all cargo that is taken in. On the outer membrane, the tail still points into the cytosol and can still reach its partners. So a receptor can go on signaling from here. A receptor with no other instruction spreads into thin tubes. The tubes pinch off, and that receptor mostly goes back to the surface.
scenes.visual: The vesicle fuses with a large round endosome and its three receptors land on the outer membrane, tails out. Purple partners touch the tails and the tails turn green. A tube grows from the endosome, one receptor slides into it, the tube tip pinches off and carries it up to a strip of surface membrane.

On the outer membrane, the tail still points into the cytosol and can still reach its partners. So a receptor can go on signaling from here. A receptor with no other instruction spreads into thin tubes. The tubes pinch off, and that receptor mostly goes back to the surface.

scenes.tts: A receptor leaves that default route when it carries a tag. The tag is ubiquitin. For an active E G F receptor, an enzyme called C B L adds it. A set of proteins on the endosome, called Escort, binds the tag. They gather the tagged receptors into a patch.
scenes.caption: A receptor leaves that default route when it carries a tag. The tag is ubiquitin. For an active EGF receptor, an enzyme called Cbl adds it. A set of proteins on the endosome, called ESCRT, binds the tag. They gather the tagged receptors into a patch.
scenes.visual: A dashed 'default route' arrow is blocked by a red bar as a gold ubiquitin badge appears. A Cbl chip hands a badge to each remaining receptor's tail. A pink ESCRT chip lands on the badges, and the two receptors slide together on the outer membrane inside a pink patch.
scenes.narration: A receptor leaves that default route when it carries a tag. The tag is ubiquitin. For an active EGF receptor, an enzyme called Cbl adds it. A set of proteins on the endosome, called ESCRT, binds the tag. They gather the tagged receptors into a patch.

scenes.tts: Escort pushes the patch inward until it pinches off as a small vesicle inside the endosome. Now ask which way the tail faces. Inside that vesicle, the tail is sealed in and cannot reach the cytosol at all. Its partners are out of reach, so the signal ends. That happens before the lysosome, a bag of digestive enzymes, destroys anything.

scenes.visual: Pink arrows push the patch inward; it deepens into a bud and pinches off as a small vesicle inside the endosome. The tails now point into the vesicle (arrows show the direction). The partners stay outside, a red bar blocks them, the tails turn red. A dashed lysosome chip appears when it is named.
scenes.narration: ESCRT pushes the patch inward until it pinches off as a small vesicle inside the endosome. Now ask which way the tail faces. Inside that vesicle, the tail is sealed in and cannot reach the cytosol at all. Its partners are out of reach, so the signal ends. That happens before the lysosome, a bag of digestive enzymes, destroys anything.

scenes.tts: Now break the sorting. In some lung cancers, the receptor M E T loses the docking site for the enzyme that adds ubiquitin. Poorly tagged, it escapes the lysosome and keeps signaling for longer than it should. The fault is not an overactive kinase, but a receptor that misses its turn. So keep this rule: taken in, a receptor can still signal, but sealed in, it cannot.

Poorly tagged, it escapes the lysosome and keeps signaling for longer than it should. The fault is not an overactive kinase, but a receptor that misses its turn. So keep this rule: taken in, a receptor can still signal, but sealed in, it cannot.
scenes.visual: A MET receptor joins the endosome with an empty, crossed docking site; the Cbl chip bounces off and no badge lands. It stays on the outer membrane, green, with partners and a clock; a crossed lysosome route, a crossed 'overactive kinase' chip and a blocked dashed vesicle show what it misses. Last, 'taken in: still signals' is set against 'sealed in: cannot'.
